questions.q: Which of these best captures the 'sharper' definition of metadata given in this lesson?
options: What makes data findable, understandable, and trustworthy without opening it first
A backup copy of the data stored in a different system
Any data that is more than one year old
The physical storage format a database uses on disk
questions.explain: The lesson's sharper definition moves past 'data about data' to the functional payoff: metadata lets you decide whether to use something before you have to open and inspect it.

questions.q: What is the most widely cited standard for structuring metadata registries, per this lesson?
options: ISO/IEC 11179
HTTP/2
ISO 8601
RFC 822
questions.explain: ISO/IEC 11179, 'Information technology â€” Metadata registries,' is the reference standard this lesson covers for structuring data element metadata.

questions.q: Which of these correctly lists the five metadata lifecycle stages in order, per this lesson?
options: Capture, store, publish, maintain, retire
Publish, capture, retire, store, maintain
Store, maintain, capture, publish, retire
Capture, maintain, store, retire, publish
questions.explain: The lifecycle moves from creation (capture) through storage, visibility (publish), ongoing upkeep (maintain), to eventual deprecation (retire).

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do organizations typically end up with more than one metadata repository?
options: Different teams adopt different tools at different times, for individually reasonable reasons
It is legally required to maintain at least three separate repositories
A single repository can only store metadata for one table at a time
Metadata repositories automatically duplicate themselves after one year
questions.explain: The BI team might pick a catalog bundled with their reporting tool, compliance maintains its own glossary â€” each choice makes sense locally, but together they create sprawl.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a business glossary deliberately leave out?
options: How a term is technically implemented â€” which column, table, or query calculates it
The name of the term itself
Who owns the term
Whether the term is approved or still a draft
questions.explain: The glossary says what a term means in business language; implementation detail (which column or query) belongs in the data dictionary, covered in Chapter 3.

questions.q: What is a 'circular definition,' per this lesson?
options: A definition that restates the term using itself or a close synonym, like 'Active: a customer who is active'
A definition that includes a diagram
A definition with more than one sentence
A definition that has been reviewed by multiple stewards
questions.explain: A circular definition only makes sense to someone who already understands the term â€” it fails exactly the people a glossary is meant to help.

questions.q: Which of these correctly lists the four term lifecycle states in order, per this lesson?
options: Draft, in review, approved, deprecated
Approved, draft, deprecated, in review
In review, deprecated, draft, approved
Deprecated, approved, draft, in review
questions.explain: A term moves from a flagged, unofficial draft, through review with rationale, to the official approved state, and eventually to deprecated once retired.

questions.q: Per this lesson's six-step process, what should come first when starting a glossary?
options: Pick one scoped domain, rather than the whole organization at once
Buy the most expensive glossary software available
Delete all existing documentation before starting
Define every possible business term in the organization simultaneously
questions.explain: A glossary for one domain, done well, is more valuable than a half-finished glossary attempting all domains at once â€” the same scoped-pilot logic from Data Governance Foundations.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what question does a data dictionary answer, as distinct from a glossary?
options: What is this specific table or column, structurally?
What does this concept mean to the business?
Who is accountable for the overall governance program?
How much does this data cost to store?
questions.explain: The glossary answers meaning; the dictionary answers physical, structural facts about a specific table or column.

questions.q: Which SQL Server feature does this lesson use to pull a table's structural metadata automatically?
options: INFORMATION_SCHEMA views
The Windows Event Viewer
A manually maintained Excel spreadsheet
The sp_helpdb stored procedure exclusively
questions.explain: Querying INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS returns column name, data type, length, nullability, and default value directly from the live schema, with no manual documentation effort.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a dictionary still need standards even though INFORMATION_SCHEMA auto-generates much of it?
options: Because the values those fields contain (like column names) can still vary wildly across tables built by different teams
Because INFORMATION_SCHEMA is unreliable and often returns incorrect data
Because standards are only needed for manually-entered fields, never automated ones
Because SQL Server requires a separate license for standardized dictionaries
questions.explain: The schema is auto-documented, but one table might use CustID and another customer_id for the same concept â€” consistency still has to be deliberately maintained.

questions.q: What is 'structural drift,' per this lesson?
options: A column gets renamed, resized, or dropped, and the documentation still describes the old shape
A column's business meaning changes while its structure stays the same
A table is backed up to a different server
A glossary term is marked as deprecated
questions.explain: Structural drift is a mismatch between the real schema and what's documented â€” directly detectable by comparing the two.

questions.q: What is a Critical Data Element (CDE), per this lesson?
options: A data element whose accuracy, timeliness, or integrity has outsized consequences if it's wrong
Any column that has a non-empty description in the dictionary
Every column in a table with more than ten rows
A column that is never allowed to be NULL
questions.explain: CDE status is a deliberately small, selective subset reserved for data where errors are genuinely expensive, not just inconvenient.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why isn't a simple yes/no CDE identification test (Lesson 16) enough on its own?
options: A real organization can have more identified CDEs than it can govern with equal intensity, so they need to be ranked
Because the yes/no test from Lesson 16 is always wrong
Because CDEs automatically lose their status after 90 days
Because only one CDE is allowed per organization
questions.explain: Forty CDEs is common at a mid-sized company â€” at that point the question shifts from 'is this critical' to 'which one needs attention first.'

questions.q: Which of these is one of the four additional fields a CDE record needs, per this lesson?
options: Source system of record
The font used to display the column in a report
The column's exact pixel width in a spreadsheet
The number of times the table has been backed up
questions.explain: The four additional fields are source system of record, validation rule reference, lineage summary, and escalation contact.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a regulator actually checking when auditing an organization's data governance?
options: Whether the organization can demonstrate control over the small number of elements that feed regulatory filings and financial statements
Whether every single column in every database is perfectly documented
Whether the organization uses a specific database vendor
Whether every employee has completed a training course
questions.explain: Regulators focus on the CDE concept from Lesson 16 â€” not universal perfection, but demonstrated control over the elements that actually matter for compliance.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a data catalog surface that neither the glossary nor the dictionary tracks on its own?
options: Usage information â€” which reports query a table, how often, and by whom
The table's exact storage cost in dollars
The physical server rack the database runs on
The names of every employee at the company
questions.explain: The glossary covers meaning and the dictionary covers structure, but usage information â€” how actively a dataset is relied upon â€” is the catalog's distinct contribution.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what single question determines a catalog's entire value?
options: When someone searches, do they find the right answer quickly?
How many total tables does the catalog contain?
How much did the catalog software cost to license?
How visually attractive is the catalog's user interface?
questions.explain: Perfect metadata that nobody can find is worthless â€” search quality is the one capability everything else is secondary to.

questions.q: What goes wrong in a catalog that relies on manual curation alone, per this lesson?
options: It ends up with silent gaps nobody notices, since nothing flags an undocumented table as missing
It becomes too expensive to maintain within one week
It automatically deletes all previously curated entries
It can only store exactly one table at a time
questions.explain: Curation-only catalogs are accurate where someone wrote something, but an undocumented table simply doesn't appear â€” there's no automatic signal that something is missing.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why did the final fix actually work three months later?
options: There was now exactly one definition, one source system, and one place to look it up â€” not because anyone got better at math
The company hired ten new data scientists
All three spreadsheets were simply deleted with no replacement
The executive report was discontinued entirely
questions.explain: The lesson's closing point is that giving one concept one home â€” not a math or skill improvement â€” was what actually resolved the recurring mismatch.
